label: Dysuria and haematuria
note:
The patient, a 49-year-old female, presented with dysuria, lower abdominal pain rated seven out of ten, and haematuria for six days. She reports unpleasant urinary odour and spotting blood in urine, with pain being central and intermittent. She denies fever, loin pain, or vaginal discharge. Past medical history includes irritable bowel syndrome. Current medications include Merbentine 200mg three times daily. She is allergic to clindamycin.

The working diagnosis is a urinary tract infection. The plan is to prescribe a three-day course of antibiotics to be collected from Knight’s Bridge Practice. The patient was advised to drink two and a half to three litres of water daily and use urine alkalinising sachets. She was instructed to monitor her temperature and return if symptoms worsen, fever develops, or urinary retention occurs.
patient:
Your appointment today
You came to see us because of pain when you pass urine. You also have pain in your lower tummy. This pain is rated seven out of ten. You have seen blood in your urine for six days. You noticed an unpleasant smell from your urine. You also have small spots of blood in your urine. The pain is in the middle of your tummy. It comes and goes. You do not have a fever. You do not have pain in your back. You do not have vaginal discharge. You have a history of irritable bowel syndrome. You take Merbentine 200mg three times a day. You are allergic to clindamycin.

Your diagnosis
Your assessment is a urinary tract infection. This is an infection in your bladder or tubes. It causes pain and blood in your urine.

Your treatment and next steps
We will prescribe a three-day course of antibiotics. You must collect these from Knight’s Bridge Practice. You should drink two and a half to three litres of water daily. You should use urine alkalinising sachets. These help with the pain.

When to contact us
Monitor your temperature. Return if your symptoms worsen. Return if you develop a fever. Return if you cannot pass urine.
summary: A patient in their forties presented with dysuria, lower abdominal pain, and haematuria for six days. The working diagnosis was a urinary tract infection. A three-day antibiotic course was prescribed alongside advice to increase fluid intake and use urine alkalinising sachets.

answers.happened: A straightforward urinary infection treated without a sample, but the patient's answers were short and several went past me: she mentioned blood twice before I confirmed it, and she asked twice how soon the prescription would reach the pharmacy. Most of the consultation was me asking and very little was her telling.
answers.learned: Closed questions get closed answers. Visible blood and a six-day history deserved a moment of explanation about why a sample was not needed now and when it would be. The practical question about the pharmacy was the one she cared about most.
answers.next: I would open with tell me about it and let her talk before the checklist, and I would explain what happens if the symptoms come back, since recurrent infection was the safety-net I gave without saying why.
